The covariation generator has no panel_conditions field to read. A sample series is detected from the observation text — three or more numbers in one sweep — and two series pair when they are the same length. Length is not comparability, which is why 37% of sampled covariation propositions set quantities of different kinds against each other.

1 pair(s) found at the pair stage did not become items: a spine edge whose two claims share one evidence node is not a pair, and ten such self-pairs were dropped across the corpus.

4The two-step items

Every item is exactly two steps: two observations the graph already links, asked so neither answers alone. Chains are these items joined end to end, in section 5 — never one long trace.

complementary — 6 items
journal_of_m_com_o10_o15
step 1 · XRD
Milled C10 pattern reproduces the C0 reflections (CeMg12, Y5Mg24, Ce2Mg17, Mg), with only a weak extra Co line (5) at ~44.5 deg
step 2 · TEM:SAED
SAED of milled C10: rings indexed Ce2Mg17 (306), Co (111), Y5Mg24 (330), CeMg12 (202)
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/phase/identity, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference followscausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
XRD (bulk powder pattern) and TEM/SAED (local nanoscale diffraction) independently index the same set of phases in milled C10 -- CeMg12, Y5Mg24, Ce2Mg17, Mg from XRD, and Ce2Mg17, Co, Y5Mg24, CeMg12 from SAED rings -- and the weak extra XRD line at ~44.5 deg is corroborated as a distinct Co phase by the separate Co (111) SAED ring. Together, a bulk-averaged technique and a local, spatially-resolved technique agree that Co appears only as its own separate crystalline phase alongside the unchanged C0 alloy phases, with no new reflections or rings indicating a Co-alloy reaction product. Cross-validation across the two techniques makes the 'Co stays a distinct phase, no new phase formed' reading more secure than either pattern would support alone.
limits
  • Neither technique nor their combination reports on chemical bonding, interdiffusion below diffraction detectability, or amorphous/interfacial reaction layers that would not produce a distinct new reflection or ring
  • SAED is from a small selected area and is not shown to be representative of the whole milled powder, while XRD is bulk-averaged and may not detect a highly dispersed or minor reaction product; combining them does not by itself prove the whole sample is free of any localized reaction, only that neither method finds evidence of one
  • The weak Co XRD line (5) is a single, faint reflection near 44.5 deg; the pairing corroborates its assignment to Co but does not by itself quantify the amount, distribution, or particle size of Co
  • This pair covers only the milled C10 state; it says nothing about phase/identity behavior after de/hydrogenation cycling

journal_of_m_com_o12_o18
step 1 · XRD
Dehydrogenated C0 and C10: Mg, CeH2.73, CeO2, YH2 reflections, no CeMg12/Y5Mg24/Ce2Mg17; Co marker at ~44.5 deg in C10
step 2 · TEM:HRTEM
HRTEM of dehydrogenated C10: Mg (101) 0.245 nm grain wrapped by carbon layers beside a CeH2.73 (111) 0.318 nm grain
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/phase/identity, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference followscausal strength descriptive
key — the combining proposition
XRD establishes, across the bulk of the dehydrogenated sample, that only Mg, CeH2.73, CeO2 and YH2 reflections are present (with a Co marker peak in C10) and that no CeMg12/Y5Mg24/Ce2Mg17 reflections appear, i.e. no RE-Mg intermetallic phase forms anywhere detectable in the bulk. HRTEM then shows, at one imaged region of dehydrogenated C10, a real-space grain with 0.245 nm spacing matching Mg (101) sitting directly beside a grain with 0.318 nm spacing matching CeH2.73 (111), with the Mg grain wrapped by carbon layers. Put together, the local lattice-resolved image corroborates that the phases XRD assigns bulk-wide (Mg, CeH2.73) are genuinely present as distinct, physically adjacent crystalline grains rather than an XRD artifact, and adds real-space morphological information -- the carbon wrapping of the Mg grain -- that diffraction alone cannot supply.
limits
  • XRD alone gives bulk-averaged phase presence/absence but no information on spatial arrangement, grain morphology, or whether phases are adjacent/wrapped by carbon
  • HRTEM alone images only one local grain pair and cannot establish that this Mg/CeH2.73 adjacency or the absence of RE-Mg phases is representative of the whole sample
  • the pairing does not by itself establish reversibility or cycling behavior -- only phase identity and local morphology in the dehydrogenated state shown in these panels

journal_of_m_com_o1_o8
step 1 · XRD
XRD: broad carbon hump at 2theta about 20-28 deg and Co reflections near 44, 51 and 76 deg
step 2 · TEM:SAED

the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about STR/phase/identity, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane FMdependency realinference followscausal strength descriptive
key — the combining proposition
XRD's ensemble-averaged phase signal (carbon hump ~20-28 deg plus Co reflections at 44, 51, 76 deg, consistent with fcc Co) and SAED's locally-resolved diffraction from the actual imaged nanostructure (spotty rings indexing to Co(111) and C(120)) point to the same two phases. Together they show that the fcc-Co and poorly-ordered/graphene-like-carbon phases detected in bulk by XRD are the same phases present within the specific particles imaged by TEM, i.e. the bulk-averaged phase identification is corroborated at the local, single-structure level rather than being an artifact of averaging over a heterogeneous mix of separately-phase-pure regions.
limits
  • Neither technique alone nor combined gives phase fractions, particle/domain size, or spatial arrangement (e.g. core-shell vs. mixed) of the Co and carbon components.
  • Neither establishes the degree of graphitic order beyond 'poorly ordered'; that qualitative character is inferred from peak/ring broadness, not measured quantitatively.
  • SAED confirms phase presence only in the specific region imaged, which may not represent the whole sample; XRD's bulk average may include regions not sampled by SAED.
  • Neither observation addresses formation mechanism, oxidation state, or whether any minor secondary Co phase (e.g. hcp) overlaps with the assigned fcc reflections.
  • No quantitative comparability is possible: XRD peak positions and SAED ring indices are both categorical structural identifiers, not measured amounts or rates that could be cross-checked numerically.

journal_of_m_com_o24_o25 key refiled after the wrong-item mixup
step 1 · PHYS:sieverts
Complete desorption at 300 C takes ~150 min for C0 but ~11 min for C10; C10 finishes in <40 min even at 280 C vs ~450 min for C0
step 2 · THERMAL:DSC
DSC endothermic MgH2 peak at 396.5 C (C0) vs 338.5 C (C10); onset 341.0 vs 267.0 C
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about PRP/value, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane otherdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength associative
key — the combining proposition
Taken together, Observation A (isothermal desorption-kinetics timing) and Observation B (DSC thermal-analysis peak/onset temperatures) show that the desorption-enhancing effect of C@Co (C10 vs C0) is not an artifact of a single measurement technique: two independent methods -- isothermal Sieverts timing and dynamic DSC scanning -- both register the same direction of change, with C10 completing desorption far faster than C0 at matched temperatures (Obs A) and C10's endothermic MgH2 decomposition peak (338.5 vs 396.5 C) and onset (267.0 vs 341.0 C) occurring at substantially lower temperature than C0 (Obs B). The pairing cross-validates that catalyst addition genuinely makes hydrogen release easier, across both a kinetic (time-based) and a thermal (temperature-based) probe.
limits
  • The two observations are different KINDS of quantity -- Obs A is a cumulative time-to-completion measured isothermally at fixed temperatures (300 C, 280 C), while Obs B is a peak/onset temperature read from what is presumably a dynamic DSC heating scan -- so they cannot be merged into one kinetic parameter (e.g. activation energy) without additional modeling assumptions not present in these panels.
  • The combination does not establish whether the improvement is a kinetic effect (lower activation barrier from the catalyst) or a thermodynamic effect (altered MgH2 decomposition enthalpy), because both the desorption-time shortening and the DSC peak/onset drop are consistent with either explanation.
  • Only two catalyst conditions (C0, C10) are compared across a handful of discrete temperatures/scan points, too few to support a dose-response relationship or a quantitative rate law, only an ordering (C10 faster/lower-temperature than C0 by both measures).
not identifiablekinetic catalytic effect (lowered activation energy) vs thermodynamic destabilization (altered MgH2 decomposition enthalpy) as the cause of the observed desorption improvement

claims n15

journal_of_m_com_o28_o30
step 1 · PHYS:PCT
PCT at 320-360 C: one flat plateau per temperature; C10 plateaus lie at nearly the same pressures as C0 (~0.15, 0.27, 0.45 MPa)
step 2 · THERMAL:DSC
DSC reaction heat 616.3 J/g (C0) vs 603.1 J/g (C10)
the question, as the solver sees itWhat does each of these two measurements establish on its own about PRP/value, and what does putting them together add that neither gives alone?
generator complementarydepth 2lane otherdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength associative
key — the combining proposition
PCT alone shows the equilibrium plateau pressures at 320-360 C are nearly unchanged by C10 addition (~0.15, 0.27, 0.45 MPa, same as C0), and DSC alone shows the reaction heat is nearly unchanged (616.3 J/g for C0 vs 603.1 J/g for C10). Neither alone covers both the pressure-based and heat-based side of the thermodynamics. Put together, two independent measurement types -- equilibrium pressure behavior (PCT) and calorimetric heat release (DSC) -- both point the same way, so the pair supports the broader claim that C10 leaves the hydride's overall thermodynamics essentially unaffected, a claim that PCT's pressure plateaus or DSC's heat value could not each fully support on its own.
limits
  • The pair says nothing about kinetics -- rate of hydrogen uptake/release -- since both PCT plateaus and DSC heat are equilibrium/cumulative quantities, not rates
  • The pair does not establish cycling stability or long-term behavior; both are single-measurement comparisons
  • PCT (plateau pressure, MPa) and DSC (specific reaction heat, J/g) are different quantity kinds -- a pressure at equilibrium versus a mass-normalized cumulative heat -- so their agreement is corroborative, not a single quantitative cross-check of the same number
  • The specific desorption enthalpy in kJ/mol is not given by either cited observation, so the pair cannot be used to state a derived enthalpy value

spine_edge — 7 items
journal_of_m_spi_o10_o22
step 1 · XRD
Milled C10 pattern reproduces the C0 reflections (CeMg12, Y5Mg24, Ce2Mg17, Mg), with only a weak extra Co line (5) at ~44.5 deg
step 2 · PHYS:sieverts
Plateau capacity at 250 C is ~5.1 wt% for C0 and ~4.56 wt% for C10
the question, as the solver sees itDoes the upstream evidence account for the downstream observation about STR/phase/identity / PRP/value? Say what the combination supports and what it leaves open.
generator spine_edgedepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength discriminating
key — the combining proposition
Putting the XRD result together with the Sieverts capacity result supports that the capacity drop from ~5.1 wt% (C0) to ~4.56 wt% (C10) at 250 C is not caused by C@Co reacting with the alloy to form a new deleterious phase: the milled C10 pattern reproduces only the same C0 phases (CeMg12, Y5Mg24, Ce2Mg17, Mg) plus a weak, separate Co line, so the alloy's own phase composition is essentially unchanged. Since the underlying phase set is preserved yet capacity still falls, the lower reversible capacity of C10 must be attributable to something other than a bulk chemical reaction/new-phase mechanism -- i.e., to the presence of the added C@Co itself rather than to alteration of the alloy.
limits
  • Does not identify the actual mechanism behind the capacity loss (e.g., dilution of the active alloy by inert C@Co mass, versus a catalytic/kinetic/surface effect of Co) -- only rules out a new-bulk-phase reaction as the cause.
  • The wt% capacity values are normalized to total sample mass, which now includes the added C@Co; a drop of this size could arise simply from diluting the active alloy with an inactive additive, independent of any chemical or kinetic effect, and the pair of observations cannot separate this from an intrinsic effect.
  • XRD only resolves bulk crystalline phases at its detection limit; it cannot rule out minor, amorphous, or surface-level interactions between C@Co and the alloy that fall below detection (consistent with only a weak extra Co line being seen), so 'no reaction' is a bulk-scale conclusion only.
  • Observation A is a qualitative/categorical phase-identity read on the as-milled powder while Observation B is a quantitative single-point capacity comparison from cycling/Sieverts testing; there is no shared quantitative axis (e.g., dose or amount of Co) linking the two, so no dose-response or magnitude relationship is established, only a qualitative-plus-quantitative pairing.
not identifiabledilution of the active alloy by the added inert C@Co mass vs. an intrinsic (surface or catalytic) effect of Co on the alloy's hydrogen capacity -- the bulk-phase XRD plus the net gravimetric capacity value cannot separate these two candidate causes of the capacity loss

key — the combining proposition

The kinetic figures (66 min C0 vs 11 min C10 at 360 C) are quoted correctly from Observation B, and the overall framing as 'consistent with' / 'co-occurs with' appropriately avoids asserting causation, so only the structural characterization is the problem.
limit[0]holdsBoth Observation A and Observation B are reported only for the C0/C10 comparison (Observation B explicitly gives '66 min for C0 and 11 min for C10'; Observation A describes only the surface distribution found, implicitly in C10). No intermediate or graded carbon-content samples are mentioned, so a two-point contrast with no dose-response claim is accurate.
limit[1]holdsObservation B specifies 'Second (diffusion-controlled) absorption stage' and 'at 360 C' — a single stage at a single temperature. The limit's claim that this alone does not show effects on earlier-stage rate or at other temperatures is directly supported by the narrowness of what Observation B measures.
limit[2]holdsObservation A is described purely qualitatively ('lie on particle surfaces, densest along edges and on some faces') with no numeric quantification of C or Co amount, so it indeed cannot be regressed against the numeric 66 vs 11 min values; the link can only be associative co-occurrence, not a demonstrated causal pathway.
limit[3]holdsBoth Observation A (EDS map) and Observation B (absorption kinetics) are reported for the same C0/C10 sample pair, so any other systematic difference between the two samples (e.g., from the carbon-addition/milling process) that is not captured by either observation would be confounded with the reported structure-kinetics link; this is a valid, appropriately hedged caveat rather than a claim contradicted by the data.

key — the combining proposition
Taken together, the EDS map (C and Co signals concentrated at particle edges/faces, i.e. carbon on the alloy particle surface with Co grains dispersed in it) and the JMAK desorption fits (eta = 1.59 for C0, eta = 1.32 for C10, both R2 > 0.98) support a proposed structure-kinetics link: the surface-carbon/dispersed-Co microstructure seen in the milled C10 particles co-occurs with a lower Avrami exponent for dehydrogenation, consistent with the carbon layer altering the nucleation-growth geometry of the desorption reaction relative to C0.
limits
  • The EDS map (panels F9a/F9b) characterizes only the C10 particle surface; there is no corresponding EDS image of C0 to confirm the surface layer is absent there, so the microstructure side of the comparison is one-sided.
  • The eta comparison spans two different milled compositions (C0 vs C10), which differ by more than the presence/absence of surface carbon (e.g., possible differences in particle size or Co dispersion introduced during milling), so the surface-carbon feature is confounded with other milling-induced changes.
  • The EDS map is a static, qualitative spatial distribution of elemental signal, not a kinetic or quantitative measurement, so its connection to a change in a fitted kinetic exponent is inferential rather than directly measured.
  • High linearity (R2 > 0.98) of each JMAK plot establishes the quality of the eta fit within a sample, not a relationship between the two samples' microstructures and kinetics.
not identifiableWhether the drop in eta from 1.59 (C0) to 1.32 (C10) is attributable specifically to the surface carbon/dispersed-Co layer seen by EDS, versus other concurrent milling-induced microstructural changes in the C10 sample (e.g., particle size or Co particle dispersion), cannot be separated from these two observations alone.

key — the combining proposition
Read together, the Arrhenius-derived activation-energy drop (130.3 to 81.9 kJ/mol, C0 to C10) and the measured desorption completion times (150 min to 11 min at 300 C; ~450 min to <40 min at 280 C) are directionally consistent: the catalyst that lowers the fitted energy barrier is the same one whose isothermal desorption curves finish far sooner at every temperature tested, supporting that the C@Co activation-energy reduction is the kinetic explanation for the observed speed-up in hydrogen release.
limits
  • Observation A is a single derived slope parameter (kJ/mol) from an Arrhenius fit; Observation B is a set of completion times (min) read off isothermal desorption curves at individual temperatures -- these are different kinds of quantities and the pairing shows consistency of direction, not a verified quantitative correspondence (no check that the 130.3-to-81.9 kJ/mol drop predicts the ~14x and >11x speed-ups seen at 300 C and 280 C)
  • the Arrhenius rate constants used to obtain Ea are themselves extracted from fits to isothermal desorption curves of the same kind as those underlying Observation B, so the two are not independent lines of evidence -- lower Ea and shorter completion time move together partly by construction rather than as separate confirmations
  • the Arrhenius equation conflates activation energy and pre-exponential factor; the evidence given cannot rule out that the faster desorption in C10 reflects a change in pre-exponential/surface or nucleation kinetics rather than (or in addition to) a true lowering of the energy barrier
not identifiabletrue activation-barrier lowering by C@Co vs. a change in pre-exponential/kinetic-prefactor (e.g. surface or nucleation) effects as the source of the faster desorption -- the Arrhenius fit cannot separate these

key — the combining proposition

limits

  • The Arrhenius comparison (panel F10) rests on only two lines/two samples (C0 and C10), which is enough to order the two Ea values but not enough to establish a dose-response or continuous relationship between particle dispersion/size and activation energy.
  • TEM gives a static, structural snapshot of particle size and spacing; Ea is a kinetic quantity extracted from temperature-dependent absorption/desorption rates over a separate temperature series, so the two measurements are not taken on the same axis and the link between them is inferred, not directly measured.
not identifiableWhether the lower Ea in C10 is attributable specifically to the density/uniformity of Co nanoparticle dispersion versus other compositional or structural differences between the C0 and C10 samples cannot be separated from this pairing alone.

the question, as the solver sees itAcross the series reported here, does the first quantity below move with the second quantity below? Give the comparison and say what it implies.
generator covariationdepth 2lane FMdependency realinference follows, weaklycausal strength descriptive
key — the combining proposition
The Co (111) ring appears in both the milled-C10 SAED pattern (with Ce2Mg17 (306), Y5Mg24 (330), CeMg12 (202)) and the dehydrogenated-C10 SAED pattern (with Mg (101), CeH2.73 (111), CeO2 (111)), while every other indexed phase changes identity between the two states. Only by comparing both patterns can one see that Co is the one phase that does not transform, supporting that C@Co persists unreacted with the alloy through milling and de/hydrogenation.
limits
  • This is two single snapshots (milled state, dehydrogenated state), not a continuous series across cycling -- it supports an ordering/comparison, not a trend.
  • SAED ring indexing is a qualitative presence/absence read, not a quantitative measure of how much Co is present or how much (if any) reacted; a small reacted fraction below SAED's detection limit would look identical to zero reaction.
  • The comparison is specific to sample C10; it does not by itself establish the conclusion for other samples in the series.
  • Ring indexing at (111) for Co could in principle also coincide with reflections from another phase of similar d-spacing; the panels alone do not rule this out.
not identifiabletrue chemical non-reactivity of Co with the alloy versus a reaction that occurred but fell below SAED's detection limit

propositionoverreachesObs A: 'SAED of milled C10: rings indexed Ce2Mg17 (306), Co (111), Y5Mg24 (330), CeMg12 (202)'; Obs B: 'SAED of dehydrogenated C10: rings indexed Co (111), Mg (101), CeH2.73 (111), CeO2 (111)'. The factual comparison (Co (111) common to both; Ce2Mg17/Y5Mg24/CeMg12 vs Mg/CeH2.73/CeO2 all differ) is accurate. But the conclusion goes beyond this: neither observation mentions 'C@Co' (a core-shell/carbon-coating claim) -- both list only 'Co (111)', a bare Co crystalline reflection, so labeling the persisting phase 'C@Co' and calling it 'unreacted' is not something SAED ring indexing (a presence/absence read of crystalline phases) can establish.
